analysis.one_liner: Requires banks and credit unions to cash government benefit checks for anyone, with cost-based fees only.
analysis.headline: The Government Check Cashing Act of 1991 never left the Senate Banking Committee and died with no vote and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required federally insured banks and credit unions to cash federal, state, and local government checks of $1,500 or less for anyone entitled to the money, without requiring them to open an account. Fees could not exceed the bank's actual cost, and credit unions would have had to cash government checks for members free. Banks that don't cash any checks for customers were exempt. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing or a vote [S2] [S3] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People who receive Social Security, veterans' benefits, welfare, or other government checks but don't have bank accounts. They currently must either pay a check-cashing outlet or convince a bank to cash the check without an account relationship. The bill would have forced banks to cash those checks at cost, with a posted notice and registration so people could pick up funds at up to three branch locations [S3]. It also let consumers demand direct deposit of recurring government checks [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Unbanked people living on government checks

how_it_helps.text: Requires each federally insured depository institution to cash government checks up to $1,500 for the person the check is written to, with no requirement to open an account and no prerequisite that discriminates against low-income people [S3].

Caps cashing fees at the bank's actual cost, including fraud losses, as determined through cost studies by the Federal Reserve, and requires credit unions that cash checks to cash government checks for members free of charge [S3].

Requires banks to post conspicuous notices explaining the service, register customers for a photo ID card usable at up to three branch offices, and face civil liability of $100 to $1,000 per violation, plus actual damages and attorney's fees, for noncompliance [S3].
Exempts banks that do not cash checks for any customers, limiting the mandate to banks already in the check-cashing business [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federally insured banks and credit unions would bear the cost of cashing government checks for noncustomers. Fees are capped at actual cost, so banks would absorb overhead and fraud losses beyond the allowed fee, which could be recovered in part through ordinary account fees spread across all customers. Check-cashing outlets that currently charge unbanked recipients a percentage of the check would lose some of that business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, credit unions, and check-cashing outlets

drawbacks.text: The mandate shifts real costs onto banks: fees can only recover verified actual costs, so banks would absorb overhead and fraud losses on cashing checks for noncustomers, costs that could ultimately be passed to other customers through general account pricing [S3].

The registration program is heavy: customers would have to apply with name, address, birth date, and signature, obtain a Board-prescribed photo identification card, and wait up to 15 days for registration confirmation before using the service, a burden for someone who just needs to cash a check [S3].
The Federal Reserve could suspend the requirements for any class of checks it deems subject to unacceptable fraud losses, a built-in weakening mechanism [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to unbanked benefit recipients is direct and substantial: immediate access to their own money without a fee above cost and without opening an account. The costs are modest and mostly administrative, and the exemption for banks that never cash checks narrows the burden. The main design weakness is the cumbersome registration and ID process, which could delay access for the very people it helps, and the Federal Reserve's authority to suspend coverage for fraud-prone check categories. On balance, a consumer-access bill with manageable costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the bill on February 7, 1991; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S5].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The Senate action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit unions were better off: the requirement to cash government checks at cost, without an account relationship, never took effect, and check-cashing outlets kept their market for unbanked benefit recipients.

for.name: Howard Metzenbaum
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OH), bill sponsor and chair of the Senate Banking Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Government Check Cashing Act of 1991 to require banks and credit unions to cash government checks at cost for noncustomers.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill and took no action — no hearing or vote — during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other senator cosponsored the bill, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have required federally insured institutions to cash government checks of $1,500 or less for anyone entitled to the money, with no account relationship required and fees capped at actual cost, and required credit unions to cash members' government checks free [S3]. Institutions could only recover verified costs, so they would absorb overhead and fraud losses. The bill died without action.
These businesses charge unbanked recipients a percentage of each government check. A free or cost-based bank alternative would have taken much of that business, but the bill never advanced [S2].
